hero.h1: How do we deliver the best training possible today?

toolkitTile.heading: Find methods, recipes and ideas for sessions

mistakes.heading: Common mistakes, and what to do instead
mistakes.status: Draft wording. Six of these have had their source checked. The rest follow the linked topic.

items.title: Ordering a course for a problem training cannot fix.
items.why: If people could do the job when it really mattered, the cause is tools, incentives or unclear expectations. No course changes those.
items.instead: Ask whether they could do it if they had to. If yes, fix the environment. If no, train.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Skill problem or will problem?

items.title: Running a one-off event with nothing before or after it.
items.why: Whether learning shows up at work depends on the manager and the workplace as much as on the session.
items.instead: Plan the manager conversation, the first use at work and the follow-up before you plan the day.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: The transfer problem

items.title: Counting attendance and satisfaction as proof it worked.
items.why: How much people enjoyed a session says little about what they learned or what they now do.
items.instead: Decide up front what people should do differently, and go and look for that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 6: Evaluation models, used critically

source.label: Alliger, Tannenbaum, Bennett, Traver and Shotland (1997), A meta-analysis of the relations among training criteria.

items.title: Teaching the AI tool without changing the work around it.
items.why: People go back to the same workflow, access and targets, so the old way of working wins.
items.instead: Pick one real workflow, redesign it with the tool, and train people on that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 7: Training people for an AI world

items.title: Filling slides with text, then reading them out.
items.why: Reading and listening to the same words at once overloads a very limited working memory.
items.instead: One claim per slide, with evidence. Say the detail; do not show it.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: The multimedia design principles

items.title: Designing around learning styles.
items.why: There is no good evidence that matching teaching to a preferred style improves learning.
items.instead: Match the medium to the content: show a process, describe a principle, practise a skill.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Drop learning styles and the other big myths

source.label: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105 to 119.

items.title: Leaving managers out of it.
items.why: What a manager expects and reinforces afterwards is one of the strongest influences on whether new skills get used.
items.instead: Give managers three things to do: one before, one during, one after.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Stakeholders, managers and the transfer environment

items.title: Cramming everything into one long day.
items.why: Study packed into one sitting is remembered less well than the same study spread over time.
items.instead: Cut the content, split the day, and come back to the key ideas later.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Make practice harder in the ways that help

source.label: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354 to 380.

items.title: Choosing the medium before the goal.
items.why: A video, an app or a headset does not teach by itself. The method does, whatever carries it.
items.instead: Start from what people must be able to do, then pick the medium that makes that practice possible.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: Choosing the medium

items.title: Writing objectives that say "understand" or "be aware of".
items.why: Nobody can observe understanding, so nobody can design for it or check it.
items.instead: Write what people will be able to do, under what conditions, and how well.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Learning objectives and alignment

items.title: Moving a classroom session onto a video call unchanged.
items.why: Video calls tire people for specific reasons: constant close-up eye contact, seeing yourself, sitting still, and working harder to read faces.
items.instead: Keep live time for interaction only. Move content to pre-work and design against the fatigue.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 4: Why remote learning tires people

items.title: Running tick-box compliance training.
items.why: It is designed to prove that something happened, not to change what people do.
items.instead: Name the behaviour that matters and measure that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 6: Measuring behaviour and results

items.title: Adding fun extras that teach nothing.
items.why: Interesting but irrelevant material pulls attention away from the point and lowers learning.
items.instead: Cut anything that does not serve the objective, however engaging it is.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: The multimedia design principles

source.label: Sundararajan and Adesope (2020), Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect. Read through the Washington State University news release about the paper.

items.title: Judging a session by how smoothly it went.
items.why: How fluent people look in the room is a poor guide to what they will remember next week.
items.instead: Check again after a delay, when the easy familiarity has worn off.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

source.label: Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), Learning versus performance: an integrative review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 176 to 199.

items.title: Assuming people will pick it up on the job.
items.why: Experience without feedback levels off. Years in a role are not the same as getting better at it.
items.instead: Build in practice at the edge of ability, with someone giving feedback.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Build practice at the edge of ability

items.title: Publishing AI-written training that nobody qualified has checked.
items.why: AI tools produce confident errors and repeat bias from their training data.
items.instead: Use AI for the first draft and keep a named person responsible for every output.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 7: Risks, guardrails and governance

items.title: Packing a retreat from breakfast to midnight.
items.why: Memory is consolidated during sleep. Long days cut into the thing the retreat depends on.
items.instead: Protect sleep and leave gaps in the schedule on purpose.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

source.label: Diekelmann and Born (2010), The memory function of sleep.

findings.heading: Findings worth designing around
findings.status: Each finding's source was opened and read in summary on 17 November 2026. Full papers have not been read.

items.title: Recalling something beats reading it again.
items.use: Open each session with a short recall task before any new content.
items.source: Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Adesope, Trevisan and Sundararajan (2017), Rethinking the use of tests: a meta-analysis of practice testing.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Designing practice

items.title: Study spread over time beats one long session.
items.use: Split a full day into shorter sessions with gaps, or add follow-ups a few days and weeks later.
items.source: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354 to 380.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Spaced reinforcement after the event

items.title: Working memory holds about four chunks at once.
items.use: Introduce new ideas a few at a time and group them before adding more.
items.source: Cowan (2001), The magical number 4 in short-term memory: a reconsideration of mental storage capacity.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Design for a very small working memory

items.title: There is no good evidence that matching teaching to a learning style improves learning.
items.use: Stop sorting people by style. Choose the medium that suits the content.
items.source: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105 to 119.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: The myths

items.title: Satisfaction scores say little about what was learned.
items.use: Keep the feedback form short and measure behaviour separately.
items.source: Alliger, Tannenbaum, Bennett, Traver and Shotland (1997), A meta-analysis of the relations among training criteria.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 6: Evaluation models, used critically

items.title: Waiting a few seconds after a question gets better answers.
items.use: Ask, then count to three in your head before you speak again.
items.source: Rowe (1986), Wait time: slowing down may be a way of speeding up!
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 4: Facilitating versus presenting

items.title: Beginners learn more from worked examples than from solving problems cold.
items.use: Show a full solved example first, then remove the support step by step.
items.source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste and Chawla (2023), A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance. Kalyuga (2007), Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Cut the load that teaches nothing

items.title: Help that suits beginners can hold experienced people back.
items.use: In a mixed room, give the experienced people the harder version, not the same support.
items.source: Kalyuga (2007), Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Cut the load that teaches nothing

items.title: How well people perform in the session is a poor guide to what they will keep.
items.use: Do not judge a method by how the room looks. Test again later.
items.source: Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), Learning versus performance: an integrative review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 176 to 199.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

items.title: People often feel they learn more from easy study than from hard practice. Often it is the other way round.
items.use: Tell learners why the harder practice is there, or they will resist it.
items.source: Kornell and Bjork (2008), Learning concepts and categories: is spacing the enemy of induction?
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Make practice harder in the ways that help

items.title: Mixing related problem types often beats practising one type at a time.
items.use: Once the basics are in, shuffle the practice so people have to work out which approach fits.
items.source: Brunmair and Richter (2019), Similarity matters: a meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Designing practice

items.title: A specific if-then plan makes follow-through more likely.
items.use: End a session with each person writing: when this happens, I will do that.
items.source: Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Designing for transfer

items.title: Sleep after learning strengthens memory.
items.use: On multi-day programmes, protect the nights and revisit yesterday first thing.
items.source: Diekelmann and Born (2010), The memory function of sleep.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

items.title: Hours of practice explain only part of expertise.
items.use: Never promise mastery from time served. Design the quality of the practice.
items.source: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014), Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Build practice at the edge of ability

items.title: Feedback on the task helps. Praise for the person does little.
items.use: Tell people where they are, how it is going and what to do next.
items.source: Hattie and Timperley (2007), The power of feedback.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Accessibility, fairness and feedback

items.title: Interesting but irrelevant extras reduce learning.
items.use: Cut the anecdote, the clip or the graphic that does not serve the point.
items.source: Sundararajan and Adesope (2020), Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: The multimedia design principles

items.title: Teams that feel safe to speak up learn more.
items.use: Show your own mistakes early, and treat a wrong answer as useful.
items.source: Edmondson (1999), Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Make it safe to be wrong out loud

items.title: Well-designed tutoring software produces moderate, real gains.
items.use: Expect a useful improvement from adaptive tools, not a transformation, and only when the design is good.
items.source: VanLehn (2011), The relative effectiveness of human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring systems.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 7: Adaptive tutoring and the honest evidence

myths.heading: Things the industry repeats that do not hold up
myths.intro: Popular claims, each traced back to where it came from, with a verdict. Flick through a few.

items.claim: "Only 10% of training transfers to the job."
items.verdict: Verdict: a repeated estimate, not a finding.
items.why: The figure traces to a 1982 article by Georgenson and has been repeated ever since. Transfer is a real problem and hard to measure, but research shows that a good deal of training does transfer.

sources.label: Ford, Yelon and Billington (2011), How much is transferred from training to the job? The 10% delusion as a catalyst for thinking about transfer. Performance Improvement Quarterly.

items.claim: "Teach people in their own learning style."
items.why: People have preferences, but studies do not show that matching teaching to them improves learning.

sources.label: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105 to 119.

items.why: The original experiments were about how people judge feelings and attitudes, such as liking. Mehrabian himself says the figures do not apply unless a speaker is talking about their feelings or attitudes.

sources.label: Mehrabian, Silent Messages: description and ordering information (author's own page).

items.claim: "It takes 10,000 hours to become an expert."
items.why: Practice matters, but less than the slogan suggests. In a pooled analysis, hours of deliberate practice explained about a quarter of the difference in games, a fifth in music and under 1% in professions.

sources.label: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014), Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis.

items.claim: "We remember 10% of what we read and 90% of what we teach."
items.verdict: Verdict: no research behind the numbers.
items.why: The percentages trace to no study. Versions of the ranking go back to the 1850s, before any research on the question. The familiar numbers were spread in the 1960s without a cited source, then attached to a misreading of Dale's cone of experience.

sources.label: Letrud and Hernes (2018), Excavating the origins of the learning pyramid myths.

items.claim: "Spend 70% on experience, 20% on social, 10% on courses."
items.verdict: Verdict: a reminder, not a formula.
items.why: The numbers come from 1980s studies in which successful executives looked back on what had shaped them. The ratio is a later summary of those accounts, not a measurement. Treat it as a reminder that experience matters.

sources.label: Association for Talent Development (2014), 70:20:10: where is the evidence?

items.claim: "Attention spans are down to eight seconds."
items.why: The figure came from a 2015 report commissioned by Microsoft and seems to describe how long people stay on a web page. A review of lecture studies found that attention varies most with the teacher, not the clock.

sources.label: Bradbury (2016), Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more?
Bradbury (2016), full text hosted on the European Commission EPALE site.

items.why: A meta-analysis of work attitudes found that differences between generations were small or close to zero. Where they appear, other factors are the likelier cause. That study covers attitudes at work, not learning.

sources.label: Costanza, Badger, Fraser and colleagues (2012), Generational differences in work-related attitudes: a meta-analysis. Journal of Business and Psychology, 27, 375 to 394.

items.claim: "AI tutoring delivers a two sigma gain."
items.verdict: Verdict: not matched by later evidence.
items.why: Two sigma was the long-held belief about one-to-one human tutoring. A 2011 review of experiments put human tutoring nearer 0.8, and intelligent tutoring systems about the same. That review predates today's AI tutors.

sources.label: VanLehn (2011), The relative effectiveness of human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring systems.

items.why: We use virtually all of the brain, though not every cell fires at once. Scans show activity across the whole brain, even during sleep.

sources.label: Centre for Educational Neuroscience, Neuromyth or neurofact: We only use 10% of our brains.

items.why: Some functions do sit more on one side, such as language on the left and attention on the right. A scan study of over 1,000 people found no sign that individuals are left-dominant or right-dominant overall.

sources.label: Nielsen, Zielinski, Ferguson, Lainhart and Anderson (2013), An evaluation of the left-brain vs. right-brain hypothesis with resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging.

items.why: The claim was about a boost to spatial thinking. A pooled analysis of about 40 studies and over 3,000 people found no evidence that listening to Mozart improves it.

sources.label: University of Vienna news release (2010) on Pietschnig, Voracek and Formann (2010), Mozart effect, Shmozart effect: a meta-analysis. Hosted by ScienceDaily.

items.why: When the well-known study was repeated, handwriting came out slightly ahead but not reliably. The authors say it is too early to call either method better.

sources.label: Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019), How much mightier is the pen than the keyboard for note-taking? A replication and extension of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014).

items.why: Growing up with technology does not make people skilled with it, or mean they need a different kind of teaching. Designing around the idea can get in the way of learning.

sources.label: Kirschner and De Bruyckere (2017), The myths of the digital native and the multitasker.

items.claim: "High satisfaction scores show the training worked."
items.why: In a pooled analysis of 34 studies, how much people enjoyed a course told almost nothing about what they learned. Ratings of usefulness did a little better, but still cannot stand in for a test.

sources.label: Alliger, Tannenbaum, Bennett, Traver and Shotland (1997), A meta-analysis of the relations among training criteria.
Alliger, Tannenbaum, Bennett, Traver and Shotland (1998), A meta-analysis of the relations among training criteria. US Air Force Research Laboratory technical report version.

myths.unwrittenWhy: This claim is on the list to trace and check. Nothing is said about it until that is done.

cases.heading: Who does this well

items.name: Commercial aviation
items.programme: Simulator and crew resource management training
items.what: Airline crews train in teamwork skills, known as crew resource management (CRM), and practise abnormal and emergency procedures together in full flight simulators. US rules require it at the start and again in recurrent training.
items.why: Crews practise rare events as a whole team in a realistic setting, are briefed before and after, and repeat the training through their careers.
items.borrow: Rehearse the rare, costly moments as a team, and put the refresher in the calendar before the first session ends.
story: CRM training teaches flight crews how to work as a team. US airline rules require approved initial CRM training before a person can serve as a flight crew member or flight attendant. Recurrent ground training for crew members must include CRM as well. The Federal Aviation Administration's guidance on CRM training is Advisory Circular 120-51E, issued in 2004 and still active.

Much of the practice happens in simulators. Under the US rules a line-oriented flight training session uses a complete flight crew and covers two flight segments typical of the airline's operation. It includes abnormal and emergency procedures and lets pilots show workload management and monitoring. The crew is briefed before and after the session. Flight crew CRM training can be completed in part or in full during such a session.

Refreshers are written into the rules. Some elements carry fixed intervals. Certain emergency drills must be done once every 24 calendar months, for example. These details come from US regulations. Other regulators were not checked for this review.
items.results: A 2008 meta-analysis of 16 CRM evaluation studies found large effects on attitudes and behaviour and a medium effect on knowledge. A 2006 review of 28 published accounts across aviation and other high-risk fields was more cautious. Trainees liked the training, effects on learning and behaviour were mixed, and the authors said the effect on safety could not be determined. Many evaluation reports also lacked the data needed to judge them.
items.limits: Full flight simulators and regulated training time are beyond most organisations. The research shows changes in attitudes and behaviour more clearly than a measured effect on accidents.

sources.label: O'Connor and colleagues (2008), Crew resource management training effectiveness: A meta-analysis and some critical needs. International Journal of Aviation Psychology.
Salas, Wilson, Burke and Wightman (2006), Does crew resource management training work? An update, an extension, and some critical needs. Human Factors.
US Code of Federal Regulations, Title 14, Part 121, Subpart N, Training Program (sections 121.404, 121.409 and 121.427).
Federal Aviation Administration (2004), Advisory Circular 120-51E, Crew Resource Management Training.

items.name: Harvard Business School
items.what: Students read a real business dilemma before class. In class the professor calls on them to say what they would do, and they debate it with each other.
items.why: People have to commit to a decision, explain it and hear it challenged. That is active work on the material, not listening to a lecture.
items.borrow: Make people commit to a decision before you discuss it.
story: Harvard Business School borrowed the idea from Harvard Law School, where Christopher Columbus Langdell had taught through cases. Dean Wallace Donham, a law graduate, pushed for it at the business school. The first business case was written in 1921.

A case is a short account of a real business dilemma. It sets out the facts and the problem but gives no answer. Harvard's own news service reported in 2008 that students prepared about 14 cases a week, alone and in study groups, and that class participation made up half the grade. The student newspaper reported in 2021 that students discuss more than 500 cases over two years.

Each class opens with a cold call. The professor picks a student to give a view, and the rest of the session is debate among students and with the professor. New teaching staff are trained in how to lead a case discussion.
items.results: The evidence is thin and does not come from Harvard. A 2024 meta-analysis of 22 studies found the case method beat lectures on knowledge and skills, but found no significant effect on motivation or attitudes. A 2014 meta-analysis of 225 studies found active learning raised exam scores by about 6% over lectures, but it covered undergraduate science, engineering and maths courses, not business cases. This review found no independent study of results at Harvard Business School itself.
items.limits: The method depends on a skilled discussion leader and on people who prepare. A director of the school's own teaching centre has said that case subjects have historically left out some races, genders and regions.

sources.label: Bayona and Durán (2024), A meta-analysis of the influence of case method and lecture teaching on cognitive and affective learning outcomes. International Journal of Management Education.
Freeman and colleagues (2014), Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Harvard Gazette (2008), From Law School to Business School: evolution of the case method.
The Harvard Crimson (2021), article on 100 years of the HBS case method.

items.name: Medical simulation centres
items.programme: Simulation-based medical education with deliberate practice
items.what: Clinicians and students practise clinical skills on simulators before and alongside work with real patients. In the strongest version the practice is deliberate, with a clear goal and repetition.
items.why: Learners can repeat a skill many times and make mistakes without harm to a patient.
items.borrow: Give people a safe place to repeat the hard part of the job, and do not count one attempt as trained.
story: Traditional clinical education relies on learning with real patients as cases come up. Simulation-based education lets learners practise on technology that stands in for the patient. Researchers have compared the two approaches since at least the 1990s.

The best-known comparison looked only at simulation that used deliberate practice. McGaghie and colleagues searched 20 years of research, from 1990 to 2010, and found 14 studies that set this kind of training against traditional clinical education.
A much wider review in the same year, by Cook and colleagues, took in 609 studies with more than 35,000 trainees across the health professions.
items.results: McGaghie and colleagues found that simulation with deliberate practice did better than traditional clinical education, with a pooled effect size of 0.71 across 14 studies. Cook and colleagues found large effects on knowledge, skills and behaviour and moderate effects on patient outcomes. That second review compared simulation with no training at all, not with other teaching. Its authors rated most studies as low quality, and results varied widely from study to study.
items.limits: The evidence is from health care, mostly for hands-on clinical skills. It says much less about whether simulation beats other active methods, and the effect on patients is smaller than the effect on test performance.

sources.label: McGaghie, Issenberg, Cohen, Barsuk and Wayne (2011), Does simulation-based medical education with deliberate practice yield better results than traditional clinical education? A meta-analytic comparative review of the evidence. Academic Medicine.
Cook and colleagues (2011), Technology-enhanced simulation for health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA.
Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, PSNet summary of Cook and colleagues (2011).

items.name: The US Army
items.what: After a training exercise the unit meets with a facilitator. Together they work out what happened, why it happened, and what to keep doing or fix.
items.why: The people who did the work find the lessons themselves, from a specific event, with several points of view and no blame.
items.borrow: After any exercise, ask the group to say what happened and why before you give your own view.
story: Before the after-action review, Army units got a performance critique. It rested on the judgement of umpires and was often a one-way, negative lecture. In the 1970s the Army Research Institute built training systems that simulated combat engagements and recorded what happened. The first of these, in 1973 and 1975, were the first to support after-action reviews. The National Training Center made the review its main feedback method when its exercises began in 1982.

A review follows a short exercise or a natural break. A trainer from outside the unit acts as facilitator. The leader restates the mission and its aims. Open questions then draw out what happened from several points of view, why the main results came about, and how to keep strengths or fix weaknesses. Platoon reviews last about 30 to 45 minutes.

The method is still current doctrine. The Army published Training Circular 7-0.1, After Action Reviews, as the first of a series that expands on its main training manual. It covers planning, running and following up a review, and both formal and informal types.
items.results: A 2013 meta-analysis by Tannenbaum and Cerasoli pooled 46 samples with 2,136 participants. Debriefs, including after-action reviews, improved performance by about 20 to 25% on average. Facilitated debriefs did better than unfacilitated ones, though only two samples had no facilitator. The studies came from many settings, not only the Army, and many did not use random assignment. An Army research report from 1999 noted that early evaluations never tested the review separately from the rest of the training.
items.limits: The evidence favours reviews led by a facilitator, so the method leans on having a capable one. Army research also found that the written take-home packages were too long and weak on concrete fixes.

sources.label: Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis. Human Factors.
US Army (2025), TMD publishes training circular to augment FM and ADP 7-0.
Morrison and Meliza (1999), Foundations of the After Action Review Process. US Army Research Institute Special Report 42.

items.name: Duolingo
items.what: A language app that teaches through short quiz-style exercises. A statistical model estimates when each learner is about to forget each word and brings it back for practice.
items.why: Recalling a word just before it fades strengthens memory more than rereading it. Spreading practice over days beats cramming.
items.borrow: Plan when each key point comes back as a recall question, and bring the shaky ones back sooner.
story: Duolingo first scheduled review with the Leitner system, a simple rule that moves an item to a longer or shorter gap depending on whether the learner got it right.

In 2016 two Duolingo researchers, Burr Settles and Brendan Meeder, published a replacement called half-life regression at a major computational linguistics conference. The model combines the classic forgetting curve with machine learning. It estimates how long each word is likely to stay in a learner's memory, using that learner's history of right and wrong answers.

They trained it on two weeks of app logs, about 12.9 million records of a learner practising a word. Its predictions of recall were at least 45 per cent more accurate than the older methods it was compared with. In a live test with millions of users, one version raised the share of learners who came back each day by about 12 per cent, and Duolingo rolled it out to everyone.

The independent study describes what this feels like for a learner. Short sessions on a phone were easy to fit in and the game features helped motivation, but a lot of time went on review and the tasks became repetitive.
items.results: The evidence for the scheduling model is peer reviewed but was written by Duolingo staff, and it measures recall prediction and return visits, not language ability. A 2012 study that found about 34 hours on the app matched a university semester was paid for by Duolingo and used a text-only test. An independent study at Michigan State University in 2019 followed nine beginners learning Turkish for 12 to 35 hours. All of them learned some Turkish, but the average score on a first-semester university test was 48 per cent and only one person passed.
items.limits: The independent study was tiny, and its learners were language researchers studying their own progress. Speaking and listening scores were lower than reading and writing, and critics say apps like this mainly build vocabulary. Spaced recall suits facts and words better than judgement or conversation.

sources.label: Settles and Meeder (2016), A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning. Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics.
Loewen and colleagues (2019), Mobile-assisted language learning: A Duolingo case study. ReCALL 31(3).
Vice (2017), Are Duolingo Users Actually Learning Anything Useful.

items.name: Khan Academy
items.what: Free online lessons and practice exercises, mostly in maths. Learners work on a skill until they show they can do it, then move to the next one.
items.why: New material builds on old. Checking that each step is secure before moving on stops gaps from piling up.
items.borrow: Set a clear pass standard for each step, check it, and give people another go before you move on.
story: Mastery learning is older than Khan Academy. The idea is to split a subject into small units, test each one, and give extra help and a second attempt to anyone who has not yet reached the standard.
Khan Academy applies this online. Learners watch videos and work through sets of practice problems, and the site records which skills each learner has reached proficiency or mastery in.

SRI Education studied how schools in the United States used it over the 2011 to 2013 school years. The study covered nine sites, 20 schools, more than 70 teachers and about 2,000 pupils a year in grades 5 to 10. Most teachers used Khan Academy to add practice to their own lessons, not to replace them.
items.results: A 1990 review of 108 controlled studies of mastery learning found exam scores about half a standard deviation higher on average, long before Khan Academy existed. The SRI study, funded by the Gates Foundation, found that more use went with better than expected maths results and lower maths anxiety, but its authors warned against reading this as cause and effect. Khan Academy's own 2022 study of 99 districts reported gains of 0.26 standard deviations for pupils who did at least 30 minutes a week. Only 4.7 per cent of pupils reached that dose, and about 9 per cent did in the company's 2022 to 2023 data.
items.limits: The usage studies are correlations, and keen pupils may both practise more and learn more. The 1990 review also found that fewer students finished self-paced college courses. Khan Academy's own research post, last updated in March 2025, reported no results yet for its AI tutor Khanmigo.

items.name: Outward Bound
items.what: Residential courses that take groups away from normal life and set them hard physical challenges outdoors, such as expeditions and sailing.
items.why: The 1997 review authors suggest three reasons: full immersion with real consequences, hard goals built to be reachable, and far more feedback than a classroom gives.
items.borrow: Set a goal that feels too hard, structure it so the group can reach it, and give feedback throughout.
story: Outward Bound began in Aberdovey on the Welsh coast in 1941. The educator Kurt Hahn developed the idea and Lawrence Holt of the Blue Funnel shipping line paid for the first course. Holt wanted young merchant sailors to have the resilience to survive at sea in wartime, so the training mixed small-boat and survival skills with character building.
The model spread to other countries within a few years and was adapted to local settings. Outward Bound in the UK says more than 1.2 million people have taken a course.
In 1997 John Hattie and colleagues pulled together 96 studies of adventure programmes such as Outward Bound. Hattie noted that much earlier writing on the subject read like promotion.
items.results: The 1997 review covered 96 studies and 151 samples. It found an average effect of 0.34 by the end of a course on outcomes such as self-concept and leadership, with a further gain of 0.17 at follow-up, which is unusual because most training effects fade. Results varied widely between programmes, and longer courses and older participants did better. The Education Endowment Foundation rates the evidence that outdoor adventure learning raises school attainment as extremely weak, based on nine studies, none independently evaluated.
items.limits: The gains are in confidence and personal skills, not in job skills or exam results. The 1997 authors could not say why the effects lasted, and the strongest results came from courses of 20 days or more, so a one-day team event should not expect the same. Cost is a barrier, with the Foundation quoting about 1,000 pounds for a ten-day sailing course.

sources.label: Hattie, Marsh, Neill and Richards (1997), Adventure Education and Outward Bound: Out-of-Class Experiences That Make a Lasting Difference. Review of Educational Research 67(1).
